statement: A pool of CAP node indices, all free at start, shared by threads that alloc and free concurrently. A node is never owned by two threads at once; alloc never returns an index outside the pool; afterwards, run alone, the pool hands out exactly CAP distinct nodes and then reports empty (nothing lost, duplicated or corrupted); the next links must be atomic (no data race); every operation returns. Premise: fewer than 2^TAG allocations overlap one allocation (a tag that wraps all the way round cannot be told apart).
contract: template<unsigned CAP, unsigned TAG> struct FreeList { FreeList(); int alloc(); void free(int i); };  alloc returns an index in [0, CAP) or -1 if no node is free (it may also return -1 under contention); free takes a node the caller owns. TAG is the width of the ABA tag: 16 in production, shrunk for verification.
instantiate: template struct FreeList<2, 2>; template struct FreeList<2, 16>;
scenario_rule: a cycler racing a hoarder (the classic ABA: pop x, pop y, push x), two cyclers racing each other, and two 2-bit-tag scenarios: one starting from tag 0, one where solo alloc/free cycles first push the tag to its wrap point (3) so the concurrent part crosses it

survivor_annotations.why: compile-time guard on CAP: CAP = 0xFFFF would also fit (index + 1 <= 0xFFFF in 16 bits); no instantiation behaves differently

compile-time guard on TAG: it would admit TAG = 17, which the packing cannot store (one tag bit would be shifted out). Every TAG the spec runs (2, 16) behaves identically; the guard itself is not part of the concurrent behaviour under test
initial tag 1 instead of 0: the starting value of an ABA tag is arbitrary, only the fact that it changes on every allocation matters
the tag counts down instead of up on each allocation; modulo 2^TAG the sequence of values is just as long before it repeats
